chapter_metadata.title: Interventional Pulmonary and Advanced Bronchoscopy Training
learning_objectives: Understand the history and evolution of IP fellowship training.
Recognize US and European training requirements and global perspectives.
Describe the role of simulation in IP education.
Differentiate between competency, certification, and credentialing.
Identify opportunities and challenges in CME and mastery development.
key_points: IP training has evolved from apprenticeship to structured fellowships with certification.
Simulation plays a critical role in competency development but lacks standardized adoption.
Procedural volume requirements differ between US (higher) and Europe (lower).
Validated assessment tools exist (RIGID-TASC, EBUS-STAT, CAPS, TUBE-iCOMPT) but are underutilized.
CME is vital as new technologies outpace traditional fellowship curricula.
chapter_metadata.reference: DeMarco B, Holden VK, Lee HJ. Interventional Pulmonary and Advanced Bronchoscopy Training. In: Yarmus L, et al, eds. Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology. Springer; 2025. doi:10.1007/978-3-031-49583-0_9-1

tables.title: Procedural volume training requirements and validated tools

figures.caption: Growth in IP fellowship education (1992–2023), milestones include AABIP founding, ERS/ATS statements, CHEST statement, AIPPD establishment, IP match, board certification, ACGME subspecialty recognition.
Five stages of IP training: theoretical stage, simulation, supervised practice, quantitative/qualitative assessment, lifelong learning.
Performance with deliberate practice over a career: deliberate practice leads to expert performance; lack of deliberate practice risks arrested development.

clinical_pearls: Simulation accelerates acquisition of bronchoscopic skills in a low-risk environment.
Competency ≠ certification ≠ credentialing — these terms must be distinguished.
Mastery requires deliberate practice and expert coaching, often continuing well beyond fellowship.
Competency-based assessment is more meaningful than procedural volume alone.

points: IP training progresses from fellowship to CME and mastery across a physician’s career.
Ongoing CME is essential due to rapid technology evolution (e.g., robotic bronchoscopy).
Mastery requires expert coaching and deliberate practice; without it, performance plateaus.
